catalog_quote: [p. x, 1.1] There is an additional phoneme of stress, indicated by an acute accent (´) over the vowel, that varies dialectically though it usually occurs on the next to the last syllable. ... [p. xi, 1.2.1] Since stress has a low contrastive function, it will be marked only when it causes a difference in meaning between two words, for example: pahid ‘wipe’ pahíd ‘shrub’ / salà ‘small cut’ salâ ‘sin’ ... [p. xiii, 2.1.6 Stress shift] With suffixation the stress shifts to the new penult of the word, for example: kágat ‘bite’ + -en = kagáten ‘bite something’ / lébeng ‘bury’ + -anan = lebengánan ‘grave’ ... [p. viii] Although there are some minimal pairs where stress is contrastive, this contrast is only indicated in the entry word. Once the word appears in a sentence or is affixed, the stress rules apply so there is no need to indicate it.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is treated as a phoneme (minimal pairs pahid 'wipe' vs pahíd 'shrub', salà 'small cut' vs salâ 'sin'), but with low contrastive function: it usually falls on the penultimate syllable, varies by dialect, and under suffixation moves to the new penult of the derived word. Contrastive stress is marked only on dictionary entry words; in sentences and affixed forms the (penult) stress rules apply.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in the Grammar Sketch or Introduction.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'varies dialectically'; final-stressed lexical exceptions to the penult default exist (pahíd, salâ) and are marked only in entry words: [p. viii] 'Although there are some minimal pairs where stress is contrastive, this contrast is only indicated in the entry word. Once the word appears in a sentence or is affixed, the stress rules apply so there is no need to indicate it.' The dictionary represents the 'more prestigious' lowland dialect (r intervocalically); inland dialect words are marked (dial.).
new_statements.identity_note: Post & Gardner 1992 describe the 'more prestigious' lowland Binukid dialect (r intervocalically), marking inland words as (dial.), and say stress 'varies dialectically'. Borres 2017 and Hermocilla-Borres 2018 describe Binukid as spoken by the Umajamnen (Umayamnon) tribe of Bukidnon. The Reid 1971 excerpt actually downloaded is Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut), a different language.

sources.quote: 'a grave accent (`) is marked over a word- or syllable-final vowel letter to indicate a following glottal stop ... whereas an acute accent (´) is used to disambiguate stress. If stress is final and a glottal stop is present, then a circumflex accent (ˆ) is used.' Restates Post & Gardner; treats stress as needing lexical disambiguation.
